children: Did a former East German Rust Belt state with a population smaller than Brooklyn's rock the foundations of Europe this weekend? That depends on whom you ask.

"Our party is shaken to its core," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared, after the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) drubbed his Christian Democratic Union in Sept. 6 elections in Saxony-Anhalt, advancing to the doorstep of its first state government. "We are all deeply shocked."
Investors took the news in stride, so far. The Dax 40 stock index and German sovereign bond yields both barely budged.
The AfD's core promise of "remigration" for immigrants, with studied ambiguity on whether that includes legal immigrants, sounds particularly ominous against the background of German history.

The party's lead in national polls shows it resonates beyond the 2.1 million-strong Saxony-Anhalt, says Almut Möller, director for European and Global Affairs at the European Policy Centre. "This is a watershed moment going to the very core of what Germany is right now," she says.

Caveats are that lead in politically fractured Germany means around 30% support, and national elections aren't due until 2029. Markets will focus meanwhile on whether the AfD surge forces Merz to alter a structural reform program that investors like better than voters. The Dax climbed by the close to 20% since Merz's CDU won the last election in February 2025. The chancellor has become the least popular in post-World War II Germany, with approval ratings below 20%.

The technocratic Merz, who spent decades as a corporate lawyer while on break from politics, has focused on long-term, slow-burn investments in defense and infrastructure, while axing a popular early retirement option and paring "unaffordable" social welfare spending, notes Eoin Drea, senior researcher at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies.
"The benefits of his fiscal stimulus have yet to filter down," Drea says.

The AfD's own economic program "remains very incoherent," he adds. A commitment to dump the euro and revive the Deutsche mark remains in the party's manifesto but has taken a way back seat to immigration and other culture war issues like less liberal "indoctrination" in schools.

AfD chairwoman Alice Weidel and Saxony-Anhalt standard-bearer Ulrich Siegmund are focusing more concretely on ending German support for Ukraine, sending Ukrainian refugees home, and warming to Moscow at least enough to get cheap Russian natural gas flowing West again. That puts them directly at odds with Merz who, in a rare flare of passion, pledged to "not budge one millimeter" on combating perceived Russian aggression.

The AfD stance is also out-of-synch with neighbors on the so-called far right. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has supported European aid to Ukraine. French presidential candidate Marine le Pen condemns Russia's invasion while supporting "a diplomatic solution."

Both women have kept their distance from the AfD, minimizing the prospect of a broad continental movement. "There's a split on the far right between those who want to be constructive and the proper extremists," Drea says. "No one really knows where the AfD will end up."

Tests of the AfD's momentum are looming Sept. 20 in state elections in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, a 1.5-million Baltic Sea province where the party is gunning to unseat Merz's Social Democratic Party coalition partners, and Berlin, where any gain on their 8% showing last time could be a show of strength.

However those turn out, staying the course and hoping benefits do filter down by 2029 isn't politically viable for Merz and his allies, Möller says. The AfD offers unrealistic populist remedies for the multiple traumas confronting German society, she assesses: U.S. President Donald Trump yanking on its military security blanket, Russia cutting off the gas, and China becoming more competitor than export mother lode. "The AfD suggests it would be easy to return to the old certainties," she says.
Merz and his coalition are offering no remedy at all that the electorate can believe, though. "The government hasn't managed to map the Germany of the future," Möller says.
